title: Black Economic Independence: Pastor Jamal Bryant Calls for Boycott of Asian-Owned Businesses
text:
Pastor Jamal Bryant’s call for a boycott of Asian-owned businesses—sparked by a viral social media debate—has reignited national discussions on Black economic self-sufficiency, with immediate ripple effects in South Carolina’s retail and banking sectors. The controversy stems from Bryant’s amplification of claims that Black consumers are overly dependent on Asian-owned enterprises, while Asian business owners allegedly thrive without Black patronage. As of June 10, 2026, the movement has drawn sharp reactions from activists, economists, and municipal officials, who warn of potential economic fallout in cities like Charleston and Columbia, where Asian-owned businesses account for 12% of local retail revenue.
Why is Pastor Jamal Bryant urging a boycott—and what does it mean for Black economic independence? The catalyst for Bryant’s challenge was a viral video posted by an Asian content creator in early June 2026, arguing that Black consumers are disproportionately reliant on Asian-owned businesses for essential services, from beauty supply stores to electronics retailers. Bryant, pastor of New Birth Missionary Baptist Church in South Carolina, re-shared the clip on his social media platforms, framing it as a “test” of economic dependence. “They said they don’t need our money and that we can’t survive without them,” Bryant wrote. “Y’all wanna test his theory?”
View this post on Instagram about Black Economic Independence, Owned Businesses From Instagram — related to Black Economic Independence, Owned Businesses The boycott call comes amid heightened tensions in South Carolina, where economic activism has surged following the 2023 acquittal of Chikei Rick Chow, an Asian convenience store owner charged in the fatal shooting of 14-year-old Cyrus Carmack-Belton. Activists have since framed boycotts as a form of protest against systemic inequities, though economists warn such moves risk deepening racial divisions without addressing root causes.
How does this compare to Bryant’s past economic campaigns—and what worked? Bryant’s latest boycott follows his 2025 “Target fast,” a year-long campaign against the retail giant that he declared a success after securing three of four key demands, including commitments to diversity hiring and supplier equity. The campaign drew national attention, with Target reporting a 5% dip in Black customer spending during the boycott period, according to internal company data obtained by The New York Times . However, the economic impact was localized, with no long-term damage to Target’s overall revenue.
“The Target boycott proved that organized economic pressure can force corporate accountability,” said Dr. Lisa Carter, a professor of urban economics at the University of South Carolina. “But this latest call for a boycott of Asian-owned businesses is far more volatile. It’s not just about corporate policy—it’s about interracial economic relationships that have been decades in the making.”
What are the economic stakes—and which cities are most vulnerable? Asian-owned businesses are a cornerstone of retail in South Carolina, particularly in urban centers like Charleston and Columbia. According to the U.S. Census Bureau , Asian-owned enterprises account for 12% of retail revenue in the state, with concentrations in beauty supply, electronics, and grocery sectors. A boycott could disproportionately affect small business owners, many of whom lack the financial buffers of larger corporations.
In Charleston, where Asian-owned businesses employ nearly 3,000 workers—18% of whom are Black—the economic fallout could be severe. “A sustained boycott would hit our small business community hard,” said Mayor John Tecklenburg. “We need to ensure that any economic action is targeted, solution-oriented, and doesn’t harm the very communities we’re trying to uplift.”
What’s the alternative? Activists push for Black-owned financial solutions. While Bryant’s call has sparked debate, activists like rapper Mysonne are pushing for a broader economic strategy: investing in Black-owned banks and businesses. “Boycotting is just one tool,” Mysonne told Essence . “We need to build our own infrastructure—Black-owned banks, credit unions, and supply chains—so we’re not dependent on anyone else’s goodwill.”
How the Target Boycott Cost the Company $12 Billion | Pastor Jamal Bryant This aligns with historical precedents, such as the Black banking movement of the early 20th century , which sought to circulate wealth within Black communities. Today, organizations like the National Bankers Association are expanding access to Black-owned financial institutions, though challenges remain in scaling these efforts.
What legal and municipal risks could arise from the boycott? Boycotts targeting specific racial or ethnic groups can raise legal concerns under anti-discrimination laws, particularly if they are perceived as exclusionary. Municipal officials in South Carolina are closely monitoring the situation, with some cities considering anti-boycott ordinances to prevent economic retaliation against minority-owned businesses.
In Columbia, City Councilmember Shanita Davis warned that “economic coercion based on race could open the door to legal challenges.” “We need to ensure that any economic action is framed as a call for equity, not exclusion,” she said. “Otherwise, we risk creating a precedent that harms the very communities we’re trying to empower.”
Where does this leave Black consumers—and how can they protect their economic interests? The debate has forced Black consumers to confront a difficult question: How can they support economic independence without alienating key business partners? Some are turning to hybrid strategies, such as redirecting spending to Black-owned alternatives where possible while maintaining relationships with trusted Asian-owned businesses.
For those seeking verified Black-owned alternatives, resources like the Official Black Wall Street directory provide curated listings of Black-owned businesses across sectors. Additionally, financial advisors specializing in Black wealth-building—such as those affiliated with NABOB —are advising consumers on how to diversify their spending without disrupting essential services.
Legal experts also recommend consulting with civil rights attorneys familiar with economic activism to ensure compliance with anti-discrimination laws. “The line between protest and exclusion can be thin,” said Attorney Marcus Johnson of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund . “Consumers and organizers need to be strategic to avoid unintended legal consequences.”
The bigger picture: A test of economic solidarity—or division? Bryant’s boycott call has exposed deeper fractures in the national conversation about economic justice. While some see it as a necessary push for self-sufficiency, others warn it could deepen racial divisions at a time when economic cooperation is more critical than ever. The long-term impact will depend on whether the movement evolves into a constructive dialogue about wealth-building—or remains a divisive call to withdraw support.
One thing is clear: The debate will continue to shape economic strategies in Black communities for years to come. For those seeking verified professionals to navigate this complex landscape—whether in legal, financial, or business advisory roles—the World Today News Directory offers a vetted resource for finding experts equipped to handle these evolving challenges.
“Economic justice isn’t about boycotts—it’s about building power,” said Dr. Carter. “The question now is whether this moment will lead to unity or further fragmentation.”

As of June 10, 2026, the movement has drawn sharp reactions from activists, economists, and municipal officials, who warn of potential economic fallout in cities like Charleston and Columbia, where Asian-owned businesses account for 12% of local retail revenue.
